topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Preserve an object’s prior state so it can be restored without making outside history code understand its private representation. Worked example: An opaque snapshot of a valid chart interval. Selection creates a private nested Snapshot containing copied integers. History owns snapshots by value and borrows the selection. Restoration leaves the snapshot reusable and history consumes a record only after restore.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Capture a valid state without exposing its private fields.
Distinguish local restoration from reversing external effects.
Design history consumption and capacity rules.

blocks.text: The originator creates a memento containing saved state. A caretaker keeps those records and chooses when to restore one. The originator interprets the record and restores its own invariants. The caretaker manages history policy rather than field-level copying. Capturing independent values is essential: references to live fields would remember future changes rather than past state.

cards.question: What problem does Memento address?
cards.answer: Preserve an object’s prior state so it can be restored without making outside history code understand its private representation. Worked example: An opaque snapshot of a valid chart interval. Selection creates a private nested Snapshot containing copied integers. History owns snapshots by value and borrows the selection. Restoration leaves the snapshot reusable and history consumes a record only after restore.

cards.question: What is Memento?
cards.answer: A saved record of object state whose details are controlled by the state owner.

cards.question: What is Originator?
cards.answer: The object that creates and interprets its own snapshots.

cards.question: What is Caretaker?
cards.answer: An object that keeps snapshots without managing their internal representation.

cards.question: What is Snapshot boundary?
cards.answer: The set of state restored together by one snapshot.

cards.question: Does the supplied first Undo restore the initial state?
cards.answer: No. Three backups were made before three changes. The newest backup holds S2, so the first undo restores S2 and the second restores S1.

cards.question: Why may History copy Snapshot but not edit its endpoints?
cards.answer: Copying preserves an entire valid saved value through public copy operations. Private fields and the private constructor prevent the caretaker from manufacturing a different endpoint pair.

cards.question: Why does History store snapshots instead of accessing Selection's private fields?
cards.answer: Selection owns the rule for creating valid saved state. History can keep and return opaque values without learning or duplicating that internal representation.

cards.question: Is this snapshot tied to the identity of one Selection object?
cards.answer: No. It holds a valid interval pair and can restore another Selection. An identity-bound snapshot would need a different contract and checks.

cards.question: Why copy the history before eviction and insertion?
cards.answer: If allocation fails while building the proposed history, the original history remains unchanged. Evicting first would lose an entry before the new one was safely stored.

cards.question: What happens when undo succeeds?
cards.answer: The most recent snapshot restores the selection, then that history entry is removed. A second undo moves to an older entry rather than repeating the same restore forever.

cards.question: When can saving a whole object be too expensive?
cards.answer: When state is very large or changes frequently. Deltas, persistent structures or explicit commands may reduce storage, at the cost of more complex restore behavior.

cards.question: What distinguishes Memento from Command undo in these chapters?
cards.answer: Memento restores saved state. Command remembers an operation and enough information to reverse it. Both can support undo but store different kinds of history.

cards.question: Why validate a pair before assigning either endpoint?
cards.answer: The relation low <= high spans both values. Partial assignment followed by rejection could leave an invalid interval even though the operation reported failure.

topics.title: The problem: remember an interval without breaking its rules
topics.summary: A chart lets a reader select an inclusive interval from zero through one hundred. The low endpoint must never exceed the high endpoint. A change sets both endpoints together, and undo should restore the previous pair. One direct approach keeps two old integer variables beside the user-interface code. That is enough for a single local operation when the state is already public. The problem appears when the selection owns private state and more callers need undo without learning how that state is stored.

blocks.text: Exposing low_ and high_ so a history manager can copy them creates two risks. A caller can change only one endpoint and leave an invalid interval. Also, adding another part of selection state forces every outside snapshot routine to change. The object that understands the rules should produce its own saved record. The history manager should store that record without reading or editing its contents. A saved record with this role is a memento, also called a snapshot.

discussion.question: An interval changes from 2:5 to 20:40. What information is needed to restore the earlier selection?
discussion.answer: The earlier pair, two and five, must have been saved. Keeping only the new pair or a reference to the changing pair does not preserve the previous state.

topics.title: Let the state owner define the snapshot boundary
topics.summary: Selection keeps low_ and high_ private. Its set operation accepts both values, validates all conditions, and changes neither member if the pair is invalid. The Snapshot nested class also keeps its two integers private. Its constructor is private, so outside code cannot construct an arbitrary invalid pair disguised as a valid snapshot. friend class Selection grants Selection access to those private members and constructor. Friendship is a specific access permission; it is not inheritance, ownership, or a promise that all surrounding classes can inspect the record.

blocks.text: Snapshot publicly supports copying. This lets a History store snapshots in a vector without seeing their fields. Selection::save builds a snapshot from the current valid pair and returns it by value. Modern C++ can construct that returned value directly in its destination; whether a small copy is removed does not change the ownership contract. The snapshot owns two independent integers, so later edits to Selection cannot change what the snapshot remembers. A snapshot that stored references to live endpoints would fail this basic requirement.

topics.title: Restoration should have a clear failure story
topics.summary: restore takes a const Snapshot& and copies both integers back. It borrows the saved record for the duration of the call and leaves that record unchanged. Because these integer assignments cannot allocate or throw, restoration cannot stop between endpoints through a C++ exception in this implementation. This is an exception-safety guarantee for local operations, not a statement that another thread cannot see an intermediate assignment. The program is single-threaded and requires external synchronization if shared.

blocks.text: The snapshot stores the entire selected interval and nothing else. It does not store the chart pixels, a mouse position, a disk file, or the number of saved history entries. Those choices form the snapshot boundary: which state is restored together. Including too little produces inconsistent restoration; including unrelated state makes undo surprisingly broad. Here any Snapshot created by any Selection can be restored into another Selection because every instance uses the same range rules. The test demonstrates that portable value policy. A per-document or per-session policy would need an identity token and an explicit rejection rule.

topics.title: The history manager keeps records without opening them
topics.summary: History borrows a Selection and owns a vector of Snapshot values. remember asks the selection for a snapshot and stores it. undo returns false for an empty vector, making the lack of history an ordinary result rather than an exceptional failure. Otherwise it restores the last snapshot and only then removes that snapshot. The order expresses a useful general rule: do not consume the recovery record before the restoration it supports has succeeded.

blocks.text: In this example restoration cannot throw, but retaining the order makes later changes easier to reason about. If snapshots later include a string or collection, restoring field by field could allocate and fail halfway through. A stronger design could build a complete proposed state first and swap it into place with a nonthrowing operation. The caretaker, the common pattern name for a history manager, should not guess how to do that. The object that owns the state must preserve its own invariants during restoration.

topics.title: A snapshot is a value, not a rewind button for the world
topics.summary: The sample saves [2,5], changes the selection to [20,40], and restores [2,5]. It also keeps a separate snapshot variable and restores it more than once. This is valid because restore does not consume the snapshot. History choosing to pop its last record is a policy of that history, not a property of all snapshots. A history can instead support named checkpoints, multiple branches, or repeated restore to one baseline. Each needs a clear rule for which records remain available.

blocks.text: Restoring an interval does not undo an exported image that was already sent to another person. A snapshot covers local state inside its declared boundary. It also does not automatically provide persistence across program runs: the program stores C++ values in memory and defines no file format. Persistent snapshots need versioned data, validated loading, and a plan for fields that change between software versions. Calling a memory snapshot a backup would mislead users unless those additional guarantees exist.

topics.title: Bound memory growth without weakening the contract
topics.summary: Unlimited history stores more records after every remember call. For two integers this seems cheap, but a rich document may hold large images or trees. A capacity limit is therefore a product choice as well as a memory choice: the user can undo only so far. The lab retains the newest three remembered states. It builds a proposed vector, removes the oldest item if necessary, appends the new snapshot, then swaps the proposed vector into place. If allocation fails before the swap, the original history remains available.

blocks.text: A complete copied snapshot is easiest to reason about but may be costly. An alternative stores only the changed values, called a delta, or uses command-specific undo as in Chapter 14. Another approach shares immutable data between snapshots. These designs can save memory but add dependencies between records or more demanding ownership rules. Measure the actual state size and editing pattern. Do not replace a few cheap copied values with a complicated history graph merely because the latter sounds more advanced.

blocks.title: Requirements
items: Maintain 0 <= low <= high <= 100.
Capture and restore both endpoints as one logical state.
Let History store records without reading their private values.

blocks.text: Selection creates a private nested Snapshot containing copied integers. History owns snapshots by value and borrows the selection. Restoration leaves the snapshot reusable and history consumes a record only after restore.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: Every Selection pair is valid before and after public operations.
A saved snapshot is unaffected by later changes to its source.
History must not outlive the Selection it borrows.
Cross-instance restore is allowed because instances share the same value rules.

blocks.text: Alternative: For one local edit, saving two old integers is enough. Command-specific inverse operations can reduce storage for large changes, but require correct reverse behavior. Shared immutable snapshots help large documents at the cost of more ownership design.

Verification: The program checks empty history, restore of both endpoints, snapshot reuse, invalid-pair rejection without mutation, boundary [0,100], and cross-instance restoration. It does not test persistence, concurrency, or allocation failures in history growth.

Maintenance: The state owner retains control of representation and valid restoration. Whenever a new field is added, review whether it belongs inside the snapshot boundary and add a restore test for that choice.

topics.title: Exercise 17.3: Diagnose a bug
topics.summary: An undo implementation pops the last record and then tries to restore it through a reference previously obtained from back(). What is wrong?

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: The referenced vector element has been destroyed.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: The reference dangles after pop_back. Accessing it is undefined behavior, even if the memory still contains old bits. Restore before popping, or first copy the snapshot into an independent local value.

topics.title: Exercise 17.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: Explain whether restoring one Selection snapshot into another should be allowed. Give both a valid policy and when you would reject it.

blocks.title: Hint

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: It is allowed here because all selections use the same coordinate range. Reject it for document-specific coordinates or ownership-sensitive resources unless the snapshot carries and validates a matching identity. Either policy can be sound when explicit and tested.

workshop.title: An opaque snapshot of a valid chart interval
workshop.problem: An opaque snapshot of a valid chart interval. Maintain 0 <= low <= high <= 100. Capture and restore both endpoints as one logical state. Let History store records without reading their private values.

steps.why: save makes independent copies of both integers.
Changing the live object does not alter the saved value.
The last record restores both fields before being removed.
The whole pair is validated before either assignment.

steps.state: Another Selection restores the saved record to [2,5].
steps.why: This design intentionally treats snapshots as portable interval values.

workshop.pitfall: Snapshot stores references to low_ and high_ instead of copied values. After setting [20,40], the alleged old snapshot also reads [20,40]. It observes current storage rather than retaining the old state.

discussion.question: A snapshot of an image editor would copy hundreds of megabytes after each keystroke. Name two alternatives and explain one tradeoff.
discussion.answer: Command-specific deltas store smaller changes but require correct inverse operations. Shared immutable image blocks let snapshots reuse unchanged data, but need clear ownership and a new block whenever content changes.
discussion.hint: Retain only changes or share data that cannot change.

workshop.alternative: For one local edit, saving two old integers is enough. Command-specific inverse operations can reduce storage for large changes, but require correct reverse behavior. Shared immutable snapshots help large documents at the cost of more ownership design.
workshop.design: Selection creates a private nested Snapshot containing copied integers. History owns snapshots by value and borrows the selection. Restoration leaves the snapshot reusable and history consumes a record only after restore.
invariants: Every Selection pair is valid before and after public operations.
A saved snapshot is unaffected by later changes to its source.
History must not outlive the Selection it borrows.
Cross-instance restore is allowed because instances share the same value rules.
workshop.maintenance: The state owner retains control of representation and valid restoration. Whenever a new field is added, review whether it belongs inside the snapshot boundary and add a restore test for that choice.
workshop.verification: The program checks empty history, restore of both endpoints, snapshot reuse, invalid-pair rejection without mutation, boundary [0,100], and cross-instance restoration. It does not test persistence, concurrency, or allocation failures in history growth.

overview.title: History holds records; Selection defines their meaning
overview.explanation: The History-to-Snapshot edge means owned value storage. History-to-Selection is a borrowed dependency. Selection can read Snapshot internals because of friendship, a C++ access rule; the creation/read arrow is a teaching dependency and does not mean Selection owns every saved snapshot.
